Synchronous errors crashing your asynchronous data pipelines is a systemic flaw in JavaScript. Here is how the new Promise.try standard eliminates block-scoping nightmares in Angular’s modern resource() loaders.

3 min read
17 hours ago

--

Press enter or click to view image in full size

I recently spent hours debugging a production issue where an Angular component crashed entirely, taking the application’s error boundary down with it.
The server had not failed. The HTTP request had not returned a 500. Instead, a synchronous utility function — which was parsing a local configuration object — threw a SyntaxError milliseconds before the asynchronous fetch call was executed.
Because this synchronous error occurred outside of the Promise chain, it completely bypassed Angular’s built-in resource.error() signal. It crashed the main thread.
Historically, we solved this by wrapping our code in deeply nested try/catch blocks. But as standardized in the latest TC39 ECMAScript specifications, there is now a native, elegant solution: Promise.try. Here is how to use it to safeguard your Angular 22 resource loaders.
